newsitem.title: USA: Clinton backs thorough probe of China funds charge.
newsitem.headline: Clinton backs thorough probe of China funds charge.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday backed a "thorough" investigation into allegations the Chinese government may have given money to the Democratic Party for the 1996 presidential election campaign.
Clinton said he had no knowledge of the allegations contained in a Washington Post report, but said "they obviously have to be thoroughly investigated."
It is illegal for a foreign government or foreigners in most cases to donate to U.S. campaigns.

"Obviously it would be a very serious matter for the United States if any country would attempt to funnel funds to one of our political parties for any reason whatever," Clinton told a news conference with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Clinton's joint news conference came shortly after the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee investigating campaign abuses voted its first 52 subpoenas for documents as Democrats protested nearly all seemed aimed at Clinton's 1996 campaign.

Committee chairman Fred Thompson, a Tennessee Republican, said objections from Democrats were just more "resistance" and again said it would be a bipartisan investigation into possible foreign influence in U.S. campaigns.
Earlier, Arizona Republican Sen. John McCain, a leading voice for campaign finance reform, renewed his call for a special prosecutor in light of the allegations about China.
He noted that he had twice asked Attorney General Janet Reno to name an independent counsel to look into allegations of campaign finance abuses and was turned down both times.

Reno argued the Justice Department was equipped to investigate the abuses itself, but McCain said two new reports should help change her mind. One is the Washington Post's report on Thursday that the department had uncovered evidence that China sought to direct contributions from foreign sources to the Democratic National Committee before the 1996 election.

The other was a report last week that former White House deputy chief of staff Harold Ickes had allegedly improperly discussed a $500,000 campaign contribution in a memo to a businessman possibly using a White House computer, telephone and fax.

Those reports, McCain said, "should compel her to appoint an independent counsel." In the House of Representatives, Representative Frank Wolf, a Virginia Republican, also asked for a special prosecutor.

Thursday's Page One article, written in part by the Post's onetime Watergate investigative reporter Bob Woodward, quoted officials familiar with the Justice Department inquiry but provided few specifics.
The Chinese Embassy denied doing anything improper.

Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick denied that the Justice Department's task force, consisting of 25 investigators, might be closer to seeking an independent counsel to take over the probe into Democratic fund-raising activities.

"The task force has standing instructions that if it finds any information that would lead it to believe that there should be an independent counsel, they're to bring this to our attention immediately. And that has not occurred in this case," Gorelick said.
McCain, with Democratic Sens. Russ Feingold of Wisconsin and Paul Wellstone of Minnesota, said the story about China should help push their campaign finance reform bill, which is stalled in Congress.
